a: Every Friday after the close it picks one of six euro index ETFs and tells you how much to buy this week (€40–200). You place the buy yourself at your broker. The site only suggests and keeps score.

q: What do I do each week?
a: Open Your plan and follow it: buy the amount shown into this week's ETF (copy the ISIN), sell nothing, and optionally hold the 3 stocks listed. It takes a few minutes once a week.

Each ETF gets a score: its 52-week return divided by its volatility, so steady gains beat jumpy ones. The current pick only changes when another ETF scores more than 0.25 higher, which avoids switching back and forth. That happens about {{sim_strategies|key=pick|switches_per_year}} times a year.

It buys more when the world market is below its record or stress gauges (VIX, financial conditions, the Sahm recession rule) are high, and less when things look stretched. Honest note: in tests since 2012 this made {{ip_buying|key=rule_world|irr}}% a year vs {{ip_buying|key=flat_world|irr}}% for a flat amount, so it's about comfort more than profit.

Sometimes. On euro ETFs since 2012 the rule made {{sim_strategies|key=pick|cagr}}% a year vs {{sim_strategies|key=us|cagr}}% for the S&P 500. On regional data since 1991 it made {{hist_rotation|key=pick|cagr}}% vs {{hist_rotation|key=US|cagr}}% for North America, so it lost there. Both are backtests; the live record started on 9 Oct 2026.

q: Do I ever have to sell?
a: No. When the pick switches, new money goes into the new ETF and you keep what you already hold. There are no forced sales, so there's less tax and fewer costs.

q: Is the market meter a buy or sell signal?
a: No. It describes how the market looks today (−100 to +100). Tests since 2012 and on US data since 1927 found it doesn't predict what comes next, so it doesn't change what you buy.

An optional side bet on single stocks, tracked three ways since 9 Oct 2026: the weekly long/short (3 strongest bought, 3 weakest shorted, all closed after one week), Keepers (long only, hold winners while they stay strong) and Keepers with a trend guard. On US data since 1991 the long/short stand-in made {{free_money_proxy_stats|key=fm|cagr}}% a year, long only {{free_money_proxy_stats|key=long|cagr}}% and the short side alone {{free_money_proxy_stats|key=short|cagr}}%, so the shorts hurt. Not free, and shorts can lose more than their stake.

"Signal" (0–1) is how good a buy a stock is right now: half market timing (today's market ranked against 90 years of history for buying the strongest stocks; 0 = worst setup since 1937, 1 = best) and half the stock's own trend (is it really rising, relative to its swings). "Stronger than 98%" ranks it against the other stocks in the index. "Very jumpy" means swings over 60% a year. Only the timing half is tested on history, and it works mainly at the extremes; it is not a guarantee.

A pretend account that puts in €1,000 every Friday: 70% in this week's ETF and 30% in its 3 strongest stocks, with 0.2% costs. It's compared with putting the same money into MSCI World, so you can see whether the extras help.

q: What does the Simulation page show?
a: Every strategy we tested on the same 2012–today data in one chart: the current rule, the previous one, the rejected variants and simply holding each index. It's all backtest, so it shows what would have happened, not what will.

q: Where does the data come from?
a: Free public sources: Yahoo Finance for ETF and stock prices, the US Federal Reserve (FRED) for the gauges, the Kenneth French data library for long history, and news feeds for headlines (titles and links only). Prices update every weekday; the pick is decided every Saturday morning. A banner appears if the data is out of date.
Backtests are before costs. The live record and the demo charge 0.2% per buy. Taxes aren't modelled at all, so check your own situation.
